A1.justification: Both PDFs present MMMU-Pro. The retained construction, evaluation settings and results can be matched reliably, and the text, figures, tables and appendices support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, OCR and CoT prompt comparisons, and qualitative analyses in Table 1 and Figures 6–9.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds OCR measurements, error and response-length analyses, human-data reanalysis, and a controlled vision-encoder experiment.

M1.justification: The three-step benchmark construction remains text-only filtering, option augmentation and vision-only presentation. The Claude 3.5 filtering and multiple human review rounds newly described in v3 elaborate the existing augmentation process; they do not establish that the benchmark was reconstructed. The encoder experiment evaluates existing architectures.

E1.justification: The academic benchmark retains six disciplines, 30 subjects and 1,730 questions in each input format. v3 adds standalone OCR transcription evaluation and uses Cambrian-1 1M instruction-tuning data for the encoder experiment. The additional subject examples do not introduce new academic domains.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Pixtral-12B and estimated human-expert comparisons. The OCR prompt comparison expands substantially from five models in v1 Figure 6 to thirteen in v3 Table 2, adding further InternVL, LLaVA-NeXT, MiniCPM and Idefics models within that experiment.

E3.justification: New protocols include normalized edit-distance OCR scoring, human-performance recalculation using 577 questions and records from 90 experts, annotation of 60 errors, and an encoder comparison fixing the Llama 3.1 8B backbone and 1M training examples. Core benchmark prompting remains unchanged. Table 1 also redefines its delta columns as separate standard/vision differences from MMMU.

E4.justification: v3 adds subject-level CoT analyses, quantitative OCR diagnostics, a 60-case error breakdown, descriptive-versus-analytical response-length analysis, and a DINOv2/SigLIP encoder comparison. Appendix J adds 30 subject-specific case studies. The original two qualitative examples remain as v3 Figures 11 and 10.

E5.justification: Appendix B introduces a statistical estimation procedure for human performance, adjusting answers without written solutions and reporting low, medium and high estimates. These are not confidence intervals. The ten filtering trials per language model remain unchanged, and model-score uncertainty estimates or formal significance tests are not added.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 model accuracies remain unchanged, including GPT-4o's 54.0% standard ten-option and 49.7% vision scores. v3 adds Pixtral scores of 33.4% and 25.0%, human estimates of 73.0%, 80.8% and 85.4%, and extensive diagnostic results. Table 3 newly reports vision accuracies of 17.4% for DINOv2 and 16.7% for SigLIP. The redefined deltas represent different comparisons, not performance changes.

T1.justification: Appendix B newly introduces a formal answer-count decomposition in Equation 1 and a human-performance estimator in Equation 2, supported by assumptions about transferring human performance across formats. v1 contains no comparable mathematical estimation argument.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contribution: a more robust MMMU benchmark through three construction steps, substantial model-performance drops, limited OCR-prompt benefits and generally beneficial CoT prompting. The added analyses do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v3 develops interpretations involving visual-cue dominance, context switching, shorter analytical responses and domain-dependent CoT benefits, alongside expanded training recommendations. New limitations acknowledge remaining shortcuts, restricted disciplines and formats, incomplete modeling of human perception, and potential bias in approximated human performance.

D1.justification: Appendices A, C and E add OCR-only and response-splitting prompts, Claude-assisted option validation, two human review rounds, and encoder details including the backbone, training data and 576 visual tokens. Appendix B documents human-data provenance and counts. Section 4 also describes a JSON-to-screenshot utility. These substantially expand the technical documentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds references and discussion involving MathVista, MathVerse, Pixtral, DINOv2, SigLIP and inference-time generation, while removing the LXMERT citation. Its central positioning as an MMMU extension addressing shortcuts and multimodal reasoning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: CoT and OCR sections exchange order, qualitative discussion is rewritten around distinct mechanisms, and dedicated error, response-length and training-guidance sections are introduced. The single prompt appendix becomes a structured A–J appendix with a contents page and subject subsections. Separate ethics and limitations statements are added.

P2.justification: The main text changes to two columns. Table 1 is redesigned with human rows, ranking arrows and different delta columns, while its overall-score column and the opening performance overview chart disappear. The OCR bar chart becomes an expanded table, and new scatter, error-distribution, response-length and subject-level plots accompany extensive appendix tables and illustrated cases.

improvement.justification: Direct OCR measurements, broader diagnostic analyses and explicit construction and encoder details improve the paper's evidential support and transparency. New reporting problems limit the gain: Table 1's delta definitions conflict with Section 3.2, and Appendix B/Table 5's low-tier input counts sum to 625 despite the stated 577-question subset, undermining reproducibility of the human estimates. The useful diagnostics and documentation nevertheless provide a limited net improvement.
